finding.claim: Unauthenticated cross-tenant user enumeration: any caller can list id and name for any org via the org query parameter.
finding.source: req.query.org (db.js:9), attacker-controlled over HTTP with no auth.
finding.sink: req.pg.query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1 (db.js:9), rows returned via res.json (db.js:10).

trace.note: app.get('/users') route, no auth middleware in this file
req.query.org passed as bound parameter to pg query
all matching rows returned to caller

finding.guards_checked: Query is parameterized, so no SQL injection (array/object values bind as single values and match nothing). No authentication or session check in file. No check that the caller belongs to the requested org. Repro not executed (no DB available): curl 'http://HOST:3002/users?org=<org-id>'. Caveat: req.pg is set outside this file; upstream auth, if any, is not visible here.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only file in the directory is db.js, so no upstream auth is visible. db.js:8 registers app.get("/users") with no auth middleware, and db.js:9 binds req.query.org directly into the query, which blocks SQL injection but not cross-tenant access. The /users handler at db.js:8-11 returns every row for the requested org to any caller.
verdict.reason: The attacker is anonymous over HTTP, and db.js:8-10 runs an unauthenticated query on the caller-supplied org and returns id and name via res.json; the parameterization at db.js:9 stops SQL injection but not authorization, and no auth or org-membership check exists in db.js. The candidate's caveat stands: req.pg is set outside this file, but the directory contains no other code that could add auth.

finding.claim: Async route handler has no error handling; a rejected promise is unhandled, so the request hangs and, on Node >=15, the process can crash.
finding.source: Any request to /users; precondition is req.pg being undefined or the query rejecting.
finding.sink: await req.pg.query(...) (db.js:9) with no try/catch and no .catch; response never sent on failure.

trace.note: req.pg undefined (not set in this file) or query rejects, producing an unhandled rejection

finding.guards_checked: No try/catch, no error middleware, no express-async-errors wrapper. Express 5 would route rejections to error handling, but Express version is unknown (no package.json). Conditional: attacker trigger is confirmed only if req.pg is missing; no attacker input found that makes the query fail.

verdict.guard_found: No try/catch or .catch around db.js:9, and no error middleware in db.js. The only guard is version-dependent: Express 5 forwards rejected async handlers to its default error handler, but no package.json exists to confirm the version. The parameterized query at db.js:9 ($1 bound to req.query.org) means attacker input cannot make the query reject.
verdict.reason: The trace matches db.js:8-11, but the attacker cannot trigger the failure: req.query.org is bound as a parameter at db.js:9, and the other precondition (req.pg undefined) is a server setup issue, not something a request controls. This is a robustness bug that depends on DB outages or misconfiguration, not an attacker-reachable flaw.

finding.claim: /file serves any file under public/ to unauthenticated callers. Traversal is blocked, but exposure depends entirely on the contents of public/.

trace.note: ROOT = path.resolve('public'), relative to process cwd rather than __dirname
reject unless p starts with ROOT + path.sep

finding.guards_checked: '..' traversal normalized by path.resolve then rejected by prefix check. Absolute paths (e.g. /etc/passwd) rejected by the prefix check. Empty name resolves to ROOT and is rejected. Array or missing name throws TypeError, yielding 500 in Express 4. Null bytes rejected by Node path/fs layer. Not verified: dotfile and symlink handling, which depend on Express send defaults and the contents of public/. No authentication on this route.

verdict.guard_found: Path containment at db.js:15 (`if (!p.startsWith(ROOT + path.sep)) return res.status(403).end();`), which is a real return-and-abort guard that runs before res.sendFile at db.js:16. Dotfile and symlink handling were not verified: Glob shows no public/ directory in the repo, and the candidate's own note defers that question to Express send defaults.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (ROOT at db.js:6, resolve at db.js:14, prefix check at db.js:15, sendFile at db.js:16), and the prefix check effectively blocks traversal and absolute-path escapes, so the only thing served is the intended contents of public/. Serving public/ anonymously is the route's purpose, and the repo contains no public/ directory or sensitive file to show that the exposure is a vulnerability. Symlinks or dotfiles inside public/ would be a separate, unshown concern.

finding.claim: /count is unauthenticated and discloses the line count of data.csv, and each request spawns an unthrottled child process. Errors are silently swallowed.
finding.source: Any HTTP request to /count. No attacker-controlled input reaches the command.
finding.sink: execFile('wc', ['-l', 'data.csv'], ...) (db.js:20) with output returned via res.send(out).

trace.note: /count route, no auth or rate limiting
execFile with constant argv, no shell, relative path data.csv resolved against cwd; callback ignores error e
res.send(out) returns stdout, or empty 200 on failure

finding.guards_checked: Command injection not possible: execFile without shell and constant arguments. No authentication, no rate limiting, no timeout on the spawned process, no error propagation. Impact is low: line-count disclosure plus resource exhaustion under request flooding.

verdict.guard_found: none. The /count route (db.js:19) has no auth middleware or rate limiting. execFile (db.js:20) uses a constant argv with no shell, so there is no injection. The callback takes `e` but never checks it, so failures send an empty 200 rather than being blocked. No guard sits between the anonymous caller and the spawn or the response.
verdict.reason: Any anonymous client can call /count (db.js:19), which spawns `wc -l data.csv` with no guard (db.js:20) and returns its stdout via res.send(out) (db.js:20), disclosing the line count of data.csv and allowing unthrottled process spawning; the claim is accurate but the impact is low.

finding.claim: Server listens on all interfaces over plain HTTP with no authentication, TLS, rate limiting, or body-size limits, compounding F1, F3 and F4 if reachable externally.
finding.sink: app.listen(3002) (db.js:23), which binds to all interfaces when no host is given.

trace.note: listen(3002) with no host argument, so binds to all interfaces

finding.guards_checked: No host restriction, TLS, helmet, rate limiting, or request size limits in this file. Actual reachability depends on deployment network config, which is not present in this directory. Configuration-level finding, low severity.

verdict.guard_found: None in db.js. There is no host argument at db.js:23, no TLS, no auth middleware, no rate limiting, and no body-size limits. The only guard in the file is the path-containment check at db.js:15, which covers /file only and does not restrict the listener.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.listen(3002) at db.js:23 has no host argument, so Node binds to all interfaces, and the absence of auth, TLS, and rate limiting matches the claim. Whether an external attacker can reach port 3002 depends on deployment network config (firewall, security group, container port mapping) that is not in this directory, so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.
